newsitem.title: USA: Clinton stumps in New York State, starts debate prep. [CORRECTED 18:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Clinton stumps in New York State, starts debate prep. [CORRECTED 18:55 GMT]

text.p: Back on the campaign trail after an inconclusive flurry of Middle East diplomacy, President Bill Clinton wooed voters in New York state on Thursday and began training for the first presidential debate.

At an airport rally attended by several thousand cheering supporters, Clinton previewed the themes he was expected to emphasise in his showdown with Republican challenger Dole during Sunday nimgnht's debate.
Clinton said that when he ran for president in 1992 "we were drifting toward the 21st Century" and "four years later, we're on the right track roaring toward the 21st Century."

"Compared to four years ago, there's a lot of good news. Ten and a half million new jobs. Average family income is up $1,600 after inflation since we passed the economic plan that our opponents said would drive the country into the ditch," he said.
The Democratic standardbearer was, in a sense, encroaching on enemy turf. Jack Kemp, Dole's vice-presidential running mate, represented the Buffalo area in Congress for more than a decade.

Saluting high school bands that turned out to greet him, Clinton joked about the frigid weather the region is famous for -- it was in the low 40s for his arrival. "The colder it is, the harder it is to play one of those instruments -- I know," the former saxaphone player said.
"But in Buffalo, this is a heat wave, right?" Clinton said.

Clinton mentioned his emergency summit with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (corrects name of prime minister from Yitzhak Rabin), Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and King Hussein of Jordan only in passing. But White House spokesman Mike McCurry rejected Republican criticism of the summit's failure to produce concrete results.
McCurry defied Dole and Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich to identify "any other course of action than the president saw" for preventing collapse of the Middle East peace process.

After the rally, Clinton flew by helicopter to the renowned Chautauqua Institution, a gated Victorian village founded more than a century ago as a vacation retreat for Methodist Sunday School teachers.
It is his training camp for the televised campaign debate that will occur in Hartford, Conn., at 9 p.m. EDT Sunday (0100 GMT Monday).
The institution is located 60 miles southwest of Buffalo on a wooded 750-acre (300 hectares) campus adjoining scenic Lake Chautauqua.
Aides said Clinton's preparations for his showdown with Dole would include a series of full-scale mock debates in which former Senate Democratic leader George Mitchell will impersonate Dole.
They said Clinton would also study briefing books and spend some time relaxing, perhaps with jogging and golf.

Campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart told reporters Clinton, who is famed for his oratorical skills, was "slightly apprehensive at this point" because Dole has been prepping for the debate while he was trying to end the violence between Israelis and Palestinians that erupted last week.
McCurry also jumped into the pre-debate political spin game, telling reporters that Clinton "feels like he has not had the time he had allotted and planned to prepare for the debates."
Sunday's debate between Clinton and Dole will be followed by a vice presidential showdown between Kemp and Al Gore on Wednesday night, and a second Clinton-Dole debate on Wednesday, Oct. 16.

Clinton enters the rhetorical fray in a strong position politically. With less than five weeks to go before the Nov. 5 election, he leads his rival by 10 to 15 percentage points or more in national opinion polls.
